RDP offers a reliable and encrypted connection, overcoming the limitations of VNC, which lacked encryption support and enforced password length restrictions. As part of this change, the following new kernel options have been introduced:

    -   `inst.rdp`{.literal}
    -   `inst.rdp.password`{.literal}
    -   `inst.rdp.username`{.literal}

Removed NVDIMM reconfiguration support during the installation process
:   The support for reconfiguring NVDIMM devices during the Kickstart and GUI installation has been removed in RHEL 10. However, you can still use the NVDIMM devices in the sector mode in the installation program.

Removed `inst.nompath`{.literal}, `dmraid`{.literal} and `nodmraid`{.literal} boot options
:   The `inst.nompath`{.literal}, `dmraid`{.literal} and `nodmraid`{.literal} boot options have been removed now and are no longer available for use.

The `inst.gpt`{.literal} boot option is now deprecated
:   The `inst.gpt`{.literal} boot option is now deprecated and will be removed in the future major RHEL release. To specify a preferred disk label type, use the `inst.disklabel`{.literal} boot option. To create GPT or MBR disk labels, specify `gpt`{.literal} or `mbr`{.literal} option respectively.

The `inst.xdriver`{.literal} and `inst.usefbx`{.literal} options have been removed

:   The graphical system for the installation image switched from the Xorg server to a Wayland compositor. As a consequence, the `inst.xdriver`{.literal} boot option has been removed. Wayland operates without relying on X drivers, making it incompatible with loading any such drivers. As a result, the `inst.xdriver`{.literal} option is no longer applicable.

    Additionally, the `inst.usefbx`{.literal} boot option, previously used to load a generic framebuffer X driver, has also been removed.

Logical volume devices in `/etc/fstab`{.literal} use UUID in the `fs_spec`{.literal} field

:   After installation, the system writes logical volume (LV) devices in the `/etc/fstab`{.literal} file by using UUID in the `fs_spec`{.literal} field. This change provides the following benefits:

    -   Ensures consistency across all device entries in `/etc/fstab`{.literal}.
    -   Supports LV or volume group (VG) renaming without changes in `/etc/fstab`{.literal}.
    -   Keeps `/etc/fstab`{.literal} valid after re-encrypting devices with LUKS.
    -   Preserves correct mapping of the root (`/`{.literal}) and other mounts across re-provisioning, even if device-mapper paths change.
    -   Offers predictable and portable configs as UUIDs are globally unique identifiers stored in the file system superblock.

### [15.2. Kickstart changes](#kickstart-changes) {#kickstart-changes .title}

Review the most notable changes to Kickstart between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Introduced a new `bootc`{.literal} Kickstart command as a Technology Preview

:   The installer includes support for the new `bootc`{.literal} Kickstart command as a Technology Preview. It enables the deployment of bootable containers. Although comparable to the existing `ostreecontainer`{.literal} Kickstart command, this implementation relies on the `bootc`{.literal} utility to manage both operating system content provisioning and boot loader configuration. You can use the command in the following way:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    # bootc --source-imgref=<transport>:<registry>/<namespace>/<name>:<tag>
    ```

    Note

    The feature does not support complex partitioning schemes that span multiple storage devices, custom mount point configurations beyond standard layouts, or installations from container registries requiring authentication.

Introduced a new `rdp`{.literal} Kickstart command for remote graphical installation

:   A new `rdp`{.literal} Kickstart command was added to enable Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP)-based graphical installations directly from a Kickstart configuration file. The command has the following syntax:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    # rdp [--username <USERNAME>] [--password <PASSWORD>]
    ```

    With this enhancement, you can configure and start a fully automated, headless RDP installation by using Kickstart commands. For complete information about the `rdp`{.literal} command and its options, see the Kickstart commands reference in the [Automatically installing RHEL](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/automatically_installing_rhel/index) guide.

Added Kickstart support for CA certificates to enable encrypted DNS configuration during installation
:   Support for the `%certificate`{.literal} in the Kickstart file is added to enable the installation of CA certificates into the installer environment and the installed system. This simplifies the configuration process and ensures that the encrypted DNS is operational after installation, reducing manual configuration and security gaps. The certificates are inlined in the Base64 ASCII format and imported through the `--dir`{.literal} and `--filename`{.literal} options. This enhancement facilitates encrypted DNS configuration as part of **Zero Trust Architecture** requirements. The encrypted DNS configuration during installation ensures secure DNS resolution from the start, improving security and compliance in automated deployments. For more information, see [Kickstart certificates section](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/automatically_installing_rhel/index#kickstart-certificates-section).

`pwpolicy`{.literal} and `%anaconda`{.literal} Kickstart commands have been removed
:   The support for the `pwpolicy`{.literal} and `%anaconda`{.literal} Kickstart commands has been removed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.

The `--level`{.literal} parameter of the logging Kickstart command is removed
:   The `--level`{.literal} parameter of the logging kickstart command has been removed. It is no longer possible to set the level of logging of the installation process.

Removed a few options of the `timezone`{.literal} Kickstart command

:   The following options of the `timezone`{.literal} Kickstart command has been removed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10:

    -   `--isUtc`{.literal}- instead use the `--utc`{.literal} option.
    -   `--ntpservers`{.literal}- instead use the `--ntp-server`{.literal} option of the `timesource`{.literal} kickstart command instead.
    -   `--nontp`{.literal} - instead use the `--ntp-disable`{.literal} option of the `timesource`{.literal} kickstart command.

The module kickstart command has been deprecated
:   Anaconda has deprecated its support for DNF modularity, and as a consequence the `module`{.literal} kickstart command has been deprecated. This might impact you if you are using modules in the %packages section of your kickstart files or the module kickstart command. This change is implemented for simplifying the installation process and ensuring a more consistent experience moving forward.

`auth`{.literal} or `authconfig`{.literal} commands are removed
:   The `auth`{.literal} or `authconfig`{.literal} Kickstart commands are removed now. As a replacement, use the `authselect`{.literal} kickstart command.

The `--excludeWeakdeps`{.literal} and `--instLangs`{.literal} options from `%packages`{.literal} have been removed
:   The `--excludeWeakdeps`{.literal} and `--instLangs`{.literal} options used in the `%packages`{.literal} section have been removed. To maintain similar functionality, use the updated `--exclude-weakdeps`{.literal} and `--inst-langs`{.literal} options instead. These replacements ensure compatibility and provide the same dependency and language control within package management.

Removed teaming options from the `network`{.literal} kickstart command
:   The `--teamslaves`{.literal} and `--teamconfig`{.literal} options used for configuring team devices in the `network`{.literal} kickstart command have been removed. To configure similar network settings, use the `--bondslaves`{.literal} and `--bondopts`{.literal} options to configure a Bond device.

The `%addon com_redhat_oscap`{.literal} Kickstart command has been removed
:   The support for the `%addon com_redhat_oscap`{.literal} Kickstart command has been removed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10. With RHEL 10, you can use more flexible and customizable approach to hardening systems by using Anaconda and Kickstart, in addition to the already existing Image Builder option. For more information, see [Performing a hardened installation of RHEL with Kickstart](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/security_hardening/scanning-the-system-for-configuration-compliance#performing-a-hardened-installation-of-rhel-with-kickstart).

### [15.3. Image creation](#image-builder) {#image-creation .title}

Review the most notable changes to image creation between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

New `bootc-installer`{.literal} image type available in RHEL `image-builder-cli`{.literal}
:   You can use the new `bootc-installer`{.literal} image type in RHEL \`image-builder-cli\`tool to create customized installer ISOs directly from container images. The resulting bootable installers remain consistent with the source container image.

RHEL image builder supports Anaconda network installer images
:   You can use RHEL image builder to create customized Anaconda network installer `.iso`{.literal} images instead of using the standard RHEL from the download pages.

The `image-builder-cli`{.literal} tool supports image creation for diskless systems
:   With the \`image-builder-cli\`tool, you can generate live images designed for Pre-Boot Execution Environment (PXE) booting on RHEL 10. You can use these system images to boot directly from a network without requiring local disk storage.

A new CLI experience for RHEL image builder is available (Technology Preview)
:   With this Technology Preview feature, you can install and use the new `image-builder-cli`{.literal} package to build an image with just one command.

WSL2 image generation support in RHEL image builder
:   You can use RHEL image builder to create images for Windows Subsystem for Linux version 2 (WSL2). Image builder generates the images in the `wsl`{.literal} format. You can deploy the images by double-clicking the image file to install it in your WSL2 environment.

A new plugin available for RHEL image builder
:   RHEL image builder `cockpit-composer`{.literal} package has been deprecated and replaced with the new `cockpit-image-builder`{.literal} package.

RHEL image builder supports creating disk images with advanced partitioning
:   You can customize partitioning in your blueprints, including custom mount options, LVM-based partitions and LVM-based SWAP, and create disk images with advanced partitioning layout.

You can inject your Kickstart files when creating ISO images
:   You can use the `[customization.installer]`{.literal} blueprint customization field to inject your own Kickstart file when building ISO image. The customization enables you to choose an attended, partial, or fully unattended installation.

The `openstack`{.literal} image type is dropped from on-premises in RHEL 10
:   RHEL image builder no longer supports the Openstack image type. You can use the `qcow2`{.literal} image type to build Openstack images.

RHEL 10 Public disk images now have predictable network interface names
:   The `net.ifnames=0 kernel`{.literal} parameter was removed from kernel arguments, causing all systems to use predictable network interface names.

RHEL 10 disk images no longer have the `/boot`{.literal} partition from prebuilt disk images

:   Disk images, such as AWS or KVM, do not have a separate `/boot`{.literal} partition, which provides the following enhancements:

    -   Prevents errors such as insufficient space on the `/boot`{.literal} partition.
    -   Disk images with `/`{.literal} on an LVM retain a `/boot`{.literal} partition.
    -   In RHEL images, this change targets confidential computing.
    -   Prevents the `/boot`{.literal} partition from running off disk space, which was often the case when `/boot`{.literal} was on a separate partition. As a consequence, there are smaller chances for operational failures.

The `squashfs`{.literal} package has been deprecated
:   The `squashfs`{.literal} package has been deprecated and will be removed in a future major RHEL release. As an alternative, the `dracut`{.literal} package now has support for mounting `erofs`{.literal}.

Updates on RHEL image builder support to build the RHEL for Edge image types
:   RHEL image builder will continue to support building Edge images for RHEL 9, but not for RHEL 10. You can use RHEL image mode to build RHEL for Edge images. See [Using image mode for RHEL to build, deploy, and manage operating systems](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/using_image_mode_for_rhel_to_build_deploy_and_manage_operating_systems/index).

`gdisk`{.literal} has been deprecated from boot.iso
:   The `gdisk`{.literal} program has been deprecated from the `boot.iso`{.literal} image type. You can still use `gdisk`{.literal} in your Kickstarts. However, for the `boot.iso`{.literal} image type, other tools are available for handling GPT disks, for example, the `parted`{.literal} utility.

## [Chapter 16. Kernel](#kernel) {#chapter-16.-kernel .title}

Review the most notable changes to kernel and boot loader between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

### [16.1. Notable changes to kernel](#notable-changes-to-kernel) {#notable-changes-to-kernel .title}

Review the most notable changes to kernel between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

`sched_ext scheduler`{.literal} for creating a custom scheduler

:   In RHEL 10, with `sched_ext`{.literal} you can create custom process scheduling code in extended Berkeley Packet Filter (eBPF) at runtime. The `sched_ext`{.literal} scheduler allows you to replace the standard kernel scheduler with your own scheduling logic to control process prioritization, resource allocation, and execution behavior.

    Red Hat does not provide support for a custom scheduler.

CFS is replaced with the EEVDF scheduler

:   The Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) is replaced with a new scheduler, Earliest Eligible Virtual Deadline First (EEVDF). This includes the following changes:

    -   `sched_min_granularity`{.literal} is now `sched_base_slice`{.literal}, and it uses the same unit. `sched_base_slice`{.literal} defines the minimum time that a task can be deferred from running.
    -   `sched_wakeup_granularity`{.literal} sets the baseline priority (as a fraction of a CPU) for all tasks on the CPU. `sched_wakeup_granularity`{.literal} is unused in EEVDF and therefore, it is removed.

    CFS and EEVDF deliver similar workload results in most cases. However, minor variations in performance might be observed because the logic of each task selection is different.

LUKS-encrypted kdump support on 64-bit x86

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, the kdump feature on systems that use LUKS-encrypted block devices supports automatic crash dumping without manual passphrase entry. Previously, when the root file system or kdump target device used LUKS encryption, the crash kernel could not access the encrypted device unless an administrator entered the passphrase on the console or configured a separate unencrypted kdump target.

    With Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, the running kernel can pass the LUKS volume key to the kdump kernel when loading it with kexec. Together with updates in kdump utilities, this change enables:

    -   Unattended crash dumping on LUKS-encrypted systems, including headless and remote deployments
    -   Using the same LUKS-encrypted device as both the root file system and the kdump target, where supported
    -   More consistent behavior between encrypted and unencrypted installations

    To use this capability, ensure that the system runs a Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 kernel that includes this change, that kdump is configured and enabled, and that the kdump target device is reachable in the crash kernel environment. For configuration details and supported scenarios, see the [Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 kdump documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/managing_monitoring_and_updating_the_kernel/configuring-kdump-on-the-command-line#running-kdump-on-systems-with-encrypted-disk).

Identifying CVEs patched only by kernel live patches

:   Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 adds Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) reporting to the `kpatch list`{.literal} output for loaded kernel live patch modules. The report lists CVE identifiers from live patches on the running kernel. This helps security and compliance teams confirm protection when the kernel version from `uname -r`{.literal} or external scanners still indicates a vulnerable on-disk kernel package.

    This change is especially useful when you delay reboots for uptime or coordinate kernel updates across many systems. When you plan an upgrade from RHEL 9 to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, review how vulnerability management and compliance workflows can use this reporting. You might need to update internal documentation, dashboards, or scanner configuration to account for CVEs remediated through live patches on the running kernel.

    For the procedure, see [Identifying CVEs patched by kernel live patches](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/managing_monitoring_and_updating_the_kernel/applying-patches-with-kernel-live-patching#identifying-cves-patched-by-kernel-live-patches).

Changes in live kernel patch build tooling (`klp-build`{.literal}) and kernel modules

:   The kernel live patch build tool (`klp-build`{.literal}) is now available in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 and is used to generate live patches from input kernel patches. As part of this change, the kernel build system uses additional `objtool`{.literal} processing when building kernel modules.

    Because of these changes, kernel modules can now have non-zero section load addresses (for example, non-zero `sh_addr`{.literal} values for `.text`{.literal} and related sections). This is different from earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux releases, where many tools assumed that kernel module sections start at address 0.

    This change can affect debugging and tracing tools that parse kernel module ELF metadata directly, such as tools based on `elfutils`{.literal} or `SystemTap`{.literal}, if they rely on the previous zero-based section address layout. To avoid unexpected failures or incorrect symbol resolution:

    -   Use versions of `elfutils`{.literal}, `SystemTap`{.literal}, and related tooling that support kernel modules with non-zero section addresses on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.
    -   If you maintain in-house or third-party tools that inspect kernel module ELF files, update them to handle non-zero section addresses correctly.

    If you rely on live patching workflows or custom tooling that processes kernel modules, test your scenarios on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 before upgrading production systems from earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux versions.

`perf`{.literal} tooling synchronized with upstream Linux 6.17

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2, the user-space `perf`{.literal} tooling is synchronized with the upstream Linux 6.17 `perf`{.literal} codebase. This change affects system administrators and developers who use `perf`{.literal} for performance analysis, profiling, and hardware event sampling on Red Hat Enterprise Linux systems.

    The rebase brings support for new and updated Performance Monitoring Units (PMUs) and events across several hardware platforms, including recent Intel uncore PMUs, new IBM Z CPU-MF counters, and additional vendor-specific platforms such as Fujitsu Monaka. As a result, the set of available events, metrics, and reporting options in `perf`{.literal} can differ from earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux major versions.

    Because of these changes, some existing `perf`{.literal} workflows might require adjustment:

    -   Event names, event aliases, and metrics that you used in earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux major versions might be renamed, deprecated, or replaced.
    -   Scripts, automation, and documentation that call `perf`{.literal} with specific command-line options or event names might need updates to match the new upstream behavior.
    -   `perf.data`{.literal} files that you collect on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 might not be fully compatible with older `perf`{.literal} versions from earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux major versions.

    Before upgrading to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2, review and test your `perf`{.literal}-based tooling and scripts in a non-production environment. After upgrading, verify available events and metrics with the `perf list`{.literal} and `perf help`{.literal} commands, and update any automation that relies on older event names or behaviors.

`perf`{.literal} tool rebased to upstream 6.18

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2, the `perf`{.literal} userspace tool is rebased to the upstream Linux 6.18 version. This rebase aligns the Red Hat Enterprise Linux performance monitoring stack with newer hardware support and upstream behavior.

    When upgrading to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2, note the following changes:

    -   New and updated Performance Monitoring Unit (PMU) events are available on supported Intel systems, including additional core and uncore events on Intel Core Ultra (WCL-U) platforms.
    -   Some event names, metric groups, and formulas have changed to follow upstream conventions. If you use scripted invocations such as `perf stat -M `{.literal}*`<metric-name>`{.literal}* or parse `perf`{.literal} JSON metrics, you must verify that the expected metrics and aliases are still present.
    -   Output from commands such as `perf stat`{.literal} and `perf report`{.literal} can differ slightly in formatting, column names, or default sort keys. Tools that parse `perf`{.literal} output might require updates.

    Before upgrading performance-sensitive environments or CI jobs that rely on `perf`{.literal}, test your existing workflows on Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 with the `kernel-6.12.0-177.el10`{.literal} build and re-baseline key measurements, because updated events and metric definitions can influence how results are reported.

`perf`{.literal} now statically links to `libbpf`{.literal}

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, the `perf`{.literal} profiling tool now links statically to the `libbpf`{.literal} library that is included in the kernel source tree, instead of using the `libbpf`{.literal} shared library from the `libbpf`{.literal} runtime package.

    This change provides the following benefits:

    -   `perf`{.literal} always uses a version of `libbpf`{.literal} that is tested together with the corresponding kernel build.
    -   API and ABI changes in `libbpf`{.literal} that are required by `perf`{.literal} can be delivered in a single kernel update, without requiring a matching `libbpf`{.literal} package update.
    -   When the kernel source RPM is rebuilt, `perf`{.literal} is rebuilt with the matching in-tree `libbpf`{.literal} code.

    For most users, this change is transparent and does not require any manual action. Existing `perf`{.literal} workflows and command-line options continue to work as before.

    However, if you relied on the `perf`{.literal} binary dynamically linking against the system `libbpf`{.literal} shared library---for example, for troubleshooting or for validating behavior against a specific `libbpf`{.literal} package version---you can no longer change `` perf’s `libbpf ``{.literal} behavior by updating only the `libbpf`{.literal} runtime package. In such cases, you must use the `perf`{.literal} tool from the kernel build that includes the in-tree `libbpf`{.literal} version that you want.

BPF subsystem rebased to Linux kernel 6.17

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, the Berkeley Packet Filter (BPF) subsystem is rebased to the upstream Linux kernel 6.17 level. This update adds new BPF features, a verifier, and performance improvements, which can change how existing BPF programs and tools behave after an upgrade from earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux major versions.

    Compared to previous Red Hat Enterprise Linux releases, the BPF rebase to 6.17 introduces:

    -   New BPF instructions and helper functions for observability and networking use cases.
    -   Stricter verifier checks for pointer arithmetic, bounds checks, and map access.
    -   Updates to BPF maps, program types, and attach points used by networking, tracing, and observability tools.

    After upgrading to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10:

    -   Some BPF programs that previously loaded might now be rejected by the updated verifier due to stricter safety checks or register state tracking.
    -   BPF-based tools that depend on earlier verifier behavior or kernel internals might require updates.

    Before upgrading, test your existing BPF programs and workflows on a non-production Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 system and rebuild BPF user-space components against the Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 toolchain and kernel headers.

Changes to AMD CCP driver support for Venice platforms

:   On AMD Venice-based systems, the AMD Cryptographic Co-processor (CCP) driver in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 is updated to recognize additional Venice PCI device IDs. As a result, CCP hardware on these systems is now correctly detected and initialized by the kernel.

    This change can affect environments that use the CCP engine for cryptographic acceleration (for example, IPsec or `dm-crypt`{.literal} workloads) on Venice platforms:

    -   Systems that previously did not expose CCP-based acceleration on Venice hardware might start using it after upgrading to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2, which can change performance characteristics of cryptographic workloads.
    -   Monitoring and capacity planning tools might report different CPU utilization profiles because some cryptographic operations are now offloaded to the CCP device.

    If you rely on specific performance baselines, hardware offload behavior, or FIPS-compliant crypto configurations, review and validate your workload performance and security policies after upgrading Venice-based systems to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2.

Intel In-Memory Analytics Accelerator support on Wildcat Lake platform

:   On systems based on the Intel Wildcat Lake platform, Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 now recognizes the PCI device IDs for the Intel In-Memory Analytics Accelerator (IAA) devices. Previously, these IAA devices might not have been detected correctly and could not be used by the operating system.

    As a result, when you run Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 on supported Wildcat Lake systems with IAA hardware, the kernel can now discover and expose the accelerator devices for supported workloads such as compression and analytics offload.

    To use these accelerators after upgrading to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 on Wildcat Lake systems:

    -   Ensure that the system firmware and BIOS are updated to vendor-recommended versions and that accelerator features are enabled in the firmware setup.
    -   Install the Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 kernel and related packages that provide support for Intel IAA on the Wildcat Lake platform.
    -   Follow your hardware vendor's documentation and the Red Hat Enterprise Linux hardware enablement documentation to configure and verify accelerator usage in your environment.

Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) driver updates for Intel DMR CPUs

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2, the Intel QuickAssist Technology (QAT) kernel driver is updated to a version based on upstream 6.18. This update enables QAT acceleration on recent Intel DMR-family CPUs and includes bug fixes that apply to all supported QAT devices.

    These changes can improve hardware-accelerated cryptography and data compression performance on systems with the listed processors. Because the driver includes multiple functional fixes, QAT behavior on existing platforms can change compared to earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 minor releases.

    When planning an upgrade to Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10.2 on systems that use Intel QAT:

    -   Verify that the kernel recognizes QAT devices after the upgrade and that QAT-based workloads complete successfully.
    -   Re-evaluate performance-sensitive cryptography and compression workloads that depend on QAT acceleration.
    -   Review any monitoring or troubleshooting tools that report QAT device or driver information, because identifiers and version details might differ from earlier Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 releases.

Updated `tpm2-tools`{.literal} and related TPM 2.0 components

:   In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, Trusted Platform Module (TPM) 2.0 tooling continues to evolve to match current hardware requirements and security practices. When planning an upgrade from RHEL 9 to RHEL 10 on Lenovo 64-bit x86 platforms, review any dependencies on the `tpm2-tools`{.literal} package and associated TPM-based workflows.

    If your deployments rely on TPM 2.0 for secure boot measurements, sealed key storage, attestation, or platform integrity checks, validate that your automation, scripts, and operating procedures remain compatible with the TPM tooling included in RHEL 10. In particular, verify behavior such as command-line options, output formats, and integration with provisioning or compliance pipelines before large-scale rollout. This reduces the risk of unexpected regressions in environments that treat TPM-backed trust as a critical part of their platform integrity and compliance strategy.

### [16.2. Notable changes to boot loader](#notable-changes-to-bootloader) {#notable-changes-to-boot-loader .title}

Review the most notable changes to boot loader between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Secure Boot `shim`{.literal} signing requirements

:   Red Hat Enterprise Linux uses the `shim`{.literal} boot loader as the first component in the UEFI Secure Boot chain. The `shim`{.literal} binary must be signed with keys that the platform firmware trusts, and `shim`{.literal} must trust the keys that sign later boot components such as `grub2`{.literal} and the kernel.

    In RHEL 10.2, the `shim`{.literal} binaries are signed with three keys, in this order:

    1.  Microsoft Windows UEFI Driver Publisher (2011)
    2.  Microsoft UEFI CA 2023
    3.  Red Hat UEFI Publisher 2024

    For a `shim`{.literal} binary to load under Secure Boot, at least one of the corresponding certificates must be enrolled in the system firmware trust store. Earlier `shim`{.literal} builds were signed only with the Microsoft Windows UEFI Driver Publisher (2011) key.

    For more information about these signatures and their impact on Red Hat Enterprise Linux Secure Boot, see the [Secure Boot Certificate Changes in 2026: Guidance for Red Hat Enterprise Linux Environments](https://access.redhat.com/articles/7128933).

Changes in trusted keys for `grub2`{.literal} and the kernel

:   Starting with RHEL 10.1, the `grub2`{.literal} and kernel binaries are signed with longer, more secure keys. To load these components, `shim`{.literal} must trust both Red Hat Certificate Authority (CA) 5 and CA 8. As a result, systems that upgrade to RHEL 10.2 must have a sufficiently recent `shim`{.literal} in the existing installation before attempting the upgrade.

    The minimum supported `shim`{.literal} levels for upgrade are:

    -   From RHEL 8: Update to RHEL 8.10 and ensure that `shim-15.8-6`{.literal} or later is installed before upgrading to RHEL 10.x.
    -   From RHEL 9: Ensure that `shim-15.8-3`{.literal} or later is installed before upgrading to RHEL 10.x. You cannot upgrade from RHEL 9.0 directly; you must be on RHEL 9.2 or later before moving to RHEL 10.x.

    If the existing RHEL 8 or RHEL 9 deployments use older `shim`{.literal} builds that do not trust both CA 5 and CA 8, `shim`{.literal} cannot verify the newer `grub2`{.literal} and kernel signatures. In such cases, systems with Secure Boot enabled will fail to start the updated boot chain.

Planning for June 2026 Microsoft certificate changes

:   Microsoft will no longer use the current Secure Boot signing key after June 2026. However, `shim`{.literal} binaries that are signed only with the Microsoft Windows UEFI Driver Publisher (2011) key continue to boot after June 2026, provided that the corresponding 2011 certificate remains enrolled in firmware. The RHEL 10.2 `shim`{.literal} binaries are also signed with the Microsoft UEFI CA 2023 certificate and the Red Hat UEFI Publisher 2024 key, which enables them to work with updated Secure Boot trust configurations.

    When planning upgrades to RHEL 10.2 on systems with Secure Boot enabled, perform all of the following actions:

    -   Verify that the firmware enrolls at least one of the following certificates:

        -   Microsoft Windows UEFI Driver Publisher (2011)
        -   Microsoft UEFI CA 2023
        -   Red Hat UEFI Publisher 2024

    -   Ensure that the installed `shim`{.literal} packages on existing RHEL 8 and RHEL 9 systems meet the minimum version requirements so that `shim`{.literal} trusts both Red Hat CA 5 and CA 8 and can load `grub2`{.literal} and the kernel binaries signed with longer, more secure keys.

    -   Review any custom boot flows that bypass the standard `shim`{.literal} binary and update them to comply with the RHEL Secure Boot trust model.

    Failure to meet these conditions might cause RHEL 10.2 systems to fail to boot under Secure Boot and might require firmware configuration changes or rework of the Secure Boot chain of trust before deployment.

Secure Boot shim signing for RHEL 10 on x86_64 and aarch64
:   Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 10 requires a signed shim binary to support Secure Boot on x86_64 and aarch64 architectures. The shim functions as the initial boot loader, verifying and loading subsequent boot components if you enabled Secure Boot. If a signed and trusted shim is not available, RHEL 10 cannot boot on systems with Secure Boot enforced. This limitation might affect deployments in enterprise and cloud environments.

## [Chapter 17. The command-line assistant](#the-command-lie-assistant) {#chapter-17.-the-command-line-assistant .title}

Review the most notable changes to the command-line assistant between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

The optional AI tool command-line assistant is now available in RHEL
:   You can install it and use the AI tool to interact with workflows to solve issues, to have access to knowledge from several Red Hat resources, implement new RHEL features, find information, and more.

The command-line assistant for disconnected environments is available as a Developer Preview
:   You can run the command-line assistant in a completely disconnected, offline, or air-gapped environment, because it does not require any external network connectivity to operate locally on your workstation or on an individual RHEL system.

The command-line assistant supports image mode for RHEL
:   You can customize your Containerfile to include the command-line-assistant package, create a disk image from a container image, and boot a system with that image. The system image has the command-line assistant preinstalled, and you can use it after you register your system with subscription-manager.

The MCP server for Red Hat Enterprise Linux is available as a Developer Preview
:   You can enable AI applications to perform context-aware troubleshooting on RHEL systems, including log and performance analysis, by using the new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for RHEL, available as a Developer Preview.

Color support for the command-line assistant
:   The command-line assistant supports color output by default, improving the output readability through increased visual contrast.

SAP Solutions documentation is available within the command-line assistant for disconnected environments as a Developer Preview
:   The Red Hat Enterprise Linux for SAP Solutions documentation is included in the command-line assistant knowledge base for disconnected environments as a Developer Preview. This inclusion provides more accurate and context-aware responses for SAP-related administrative and configuration tasks.

## [Chapter 18. Networking](#networking) {#chapter-18.-networking .title}

Review the most notable changes to networking between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Network team driver was removed

:   The `teamd`{.literal} service and the `libteam`{.literal} library were removed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10. As a replacement, configure a bond instead of a network team.

    Red Hat focuses its efforts on kernel-based bonding to avoid maintaining two features, bonds and teams, that have similar functions. The bonding code has a high customer adoption, is robust, and has an active community development. As a result, the bonding code receives enhancements and updates.

    If you use RHEL 9 with a network team and plan to upgrade to RHEL 10, [migrate the network team configuration to network bond](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/9/html/configuring_and_managing_networking/configuring-network-teaming_configuring-and-managing-networking#proc_migrating-a-network-team-configuration-to-network-bond_configuring-network-teaming) before you upgrade.

Removed support for network configuration files in the ifcfg format
:   Starting with RHEL 9.0, RHEL stored newly created network configurations in a key file format in the `/etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/`{.literal} directory. The connections, for which the configurations had already been stored from previous times in the `/etc/sysconfig/network-scripts/`{.literal} directory in the old ifcfg format still worked uninterrupted. However, with the RHEL 10 release, the support for the ifcfg format based network configuration files was removed.

The `dhclient`{.literal} utility was removed
:   The `dhclient`{.literal} utility is a client program used to obtain IP addresses, network configuration, and other information from a DHCP server. Since `dhclient`{.literal} is no longer developed as of early 2022, the utility was removed in Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10. As a consequence of the removal, you can no longer set `dhcp=dhclient`{.literal} in `/etc/NetworkManager.conf`{.literal}. As a replacement, use the `dhcp=internal`{.literal} (default) in your NetworkManager configuration.

Removed NIC device drivers related to iPXE

:   Internet Preboot eXecution Environment (iPXE) firmware provides a range of boot options over a network often used in environments, where machines need to boot remotely. Among others, it contains a large number of device drivers. With the RHEL 10 release, the following will be removed:

    -   The complete `ipxe-roms`{.literal} sub-RPM package

    -   Binary files containing device drivers from `ipxe-bootimgs-x86`{.literal} sub-RPM package:

        -   `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe-i386.efi`{.literal}
        -   `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe-x86_64.efi`{.literal}
        -   `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe.dsk`{.literal}
        -   `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe.iso`{.literal}
        -   `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe.lkrn`{.literal}
        -   `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe.usb`{.literal}

    Instead, iPXE now depends on the platform firmware to provide a NIC driver for the network boot. The `/usr/share/ipxe/ipxe-snponly-x86_64.efi`{.literal} and `/usr/share/ipxe/undionly.kpxe`{.literal} iPXE binary files are the part of the `ipxe-bootimgs`{.literal} package and use the NIC driver provided by the platform firmware.

`NetworkManager-initscripts-updown`{.literal} is not available
:   The `NetworkManager-initscripts-updown`{.literal} sub-package is removed in RHEL 10 because the related `network-scripts`{.literal} package had already been removed in RHEL 9.

Moving some kernel modules to `kernel-modules-extra`{.literal}

:   All kernel modules related to the following utilities have been moved to the `kernel-modules-extra`{.literal} package:

    -   `iptables`{.literal}
    -   `ip6tables`{.literal}
    -   `ipset`{.literal}
    -   `ebtables`{.literal}
    -   `arptables`{.literal}

ATM encapsulation has been removed
:   Asynchronous Transfer Mode (ATM) encapsulation enables Layer-2 (Point-to-Point Protocol, Ethernet) or Layer-3 (IP) connectivity for the ATM Adaptation Layer 5 (AAL-5). In RHEL 9, the ATM implementation was unsupported and deprecated. In RHEL 10, the kernel feature has been disabled in the kernel, and ATM is no longer available.

The `PF_KEYv2`{.literal} kernel API has been removed
:   In earlier RHEL versions, applications could configure the kernel's IPsec implementation by using the deprecated `PV_KEYv2`{.literal} and the newer `netlink`{.literal} API. `PV_KEYv2`{.literal} has not been actively maintained upstream and is missing important security features, such as modern ciphers, offload, and extended sequence number support. As a result, the `PV_KEYv2`{.literal} API has been removed in RHEL 10. If you used this kernel API in applications, migrate your applications to use the modern `netlink`{.literal} API as an alternative.

The `firewalld`{.literal} lockdown feature has been removed
:   The `firewalld`{.literal} lockdown feature could not prevent processes that are running as `root`{.literal} from adding themselves to the allow list. In RHEL 10, this feature has been removed.

The `firewalld`{.literal} service supports policy sets

:   This enhancements adds support for policy sets to the `firewalld`{.literal} service. Policy sets are collections of pre-defined policies that you can use as a starting point for certain configurations. For example, the `gateway`{.literal} policy set is a set of configurations that enable masquerading, connection tracking helpers, and forwarding between zones.

    For further details, see [Using `firewalld`{.literal} policy sets to configure a router](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/configuring_firewalls_and_packet_filters/using-and-configuring-firewalld#using-firewalld-policy-sets-to-configure-a-router).

The `nftables`{.literal} framework supports name-based `netdev`{.literal} hooks with wildcards

:   This enhancement introduces name-based `netdev`{.literal} hooks with wildcard support to the `nftables`{.literal} kernel component. This ensures defined rule sets remain stable regardless of interface presence. Previously, `nftables`{.literal} would bind to each specified interface immediately upon adding a `flowtable`{.literal} or `netdev`{.literal}-family chain. Consequently, the transaction failed due to a non-existing interface, and removing an interface deleted the matching interface specifications or entire bound chains.

    With this update, hooks for non-existing interfaces are accepted in an inactive state and bind to matching interfaces at the time they appear in the system. This dynamic registration also provides the possibility to accept simple interface (suffix) wildcards to bind a `flowtable`{.literal} or `netdev`{.literal}-family chain to any matching interface. You can inspect currently active hooks by using the `nft list hooks`{.literal} command.

Threaded NAPI busy polling support added

:   In RHEL 10.2 and later, you can enable threaded NAPI busy polling to significantly reduce the network latency. This feature uses dedicated kernel threads to continuously check for incoming packets, rather than waiting for hardware interrupts.

    By design, threaded NAPI busy polling consumes more CPU cycles to achieve higher performance and lower latency, as the CPU remains active to process data immediately. Threaded NAPI busy polling is beneficial for high-performance, low latency applications, for example applications that use the `AF_XDP`{.literal} socket. Use this enhancement for workloads where predictable, sub-microsecond response times are critical.

## [Chapter 19. Performance](#performance) {#chapter-19.-performance .title}

Review the most notable changes to performance between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

RHEL is equipped with `dyninst`{.literal} version 13.0.0

:   The `dyninst`{.literal} framework is rebased to upstream version 13.0.0 This version offers the following list of enhancements:

    -   Improved support for AMD GPU binaries

    -   Improved parsing of x86 instructions and C++ DWARF constructs

        For more information, see the [upstream documentation](https://www.mail-archive.com/dyninst-api@cs.wisc.edu/msg04522.html).

RHEL is equipped with `SystemTap`{.literal} version 5.3
:   SystemTap is rebased to version 5.3, and its multithreaded parsing capability improves startup performance by reducing initialization time by several seconds.

## [Chapter 20. Security](#security) {#chapter-20.-security .title}

Review the most notable changes to security between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

### [20.1. Security compliance changes](#security-compliance-changes-in-rhel-10) {#security-compliance-changes .title}

Review the most notable changes to security compliance between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Installation hardening with OSCAP Anaconda Addon removed
:   The `oscap-anaconda-addon`{.literal} package has been removed. As a consequence, the RHEL 10 installer no longer provides the Security Policy spoke and installation hardening. RHEL 10 introduces a more flexible and customizable approach to hardening systems by using Anaconda and Kickstart in addition to the already existing Image Builder option. For more information, see [Creating pre-hardened images with RHEL image builder OpenSCAP integration](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/security_hardening/scanning-the-system-for-configuration-compliance#performing-a-hardened-installation-of-rhel-with-kickstart).

OpenSCAP

:   The new version 1.4.x of the OpenSCAP scanner is provided in RHEL 10. The most important changes are the following:

    -   The `openscap`{.literal} package no longer provides the `openscap-devel`{.literal} subpackage for the `libopenscap`{.literal} library, which is now an internal library without public API and any guarantee for backward compatibility. The `openscap`{.literal} package is provided with no guarantee of ABI and API compatibility.

    -   The following `ds`{.literal} submodules that provide data stream composing functions have been removed from the `oscap`{.literal} tool:

        -   `sds-compose`{.literal}
        -   `sds-add`{.literal}
        -   `sds-split`{.literal}
        -   `rds-create`{.literal}
        -   `rds-split`{.literal}

    -   The following incomplete modules have been removed:

        -   `cve`{.literal}
        -   `cvss`{.literal}
        -   `cvrf`{.literal}

    -   The following deprecated command-line options have been removed:

        -   `--template`{.literal}
        -   `--oval-template`{.literal}
        -   `--sce-template`{.literal}
        -   `--skip-valid`{.literal} is removed and is replaced by `--skip-validation`{.literal}

    -   New Kickstart remediation type was added.

    -   The `autotailor`{.literal} tool now can produce XCCDF tailoring files based on JSON Tailoring.

SCAP Workbench
:   The `scap-workbench`{.literal} package with the SCAP Workbench GUI utility has been removed. As alternatives, you can use the `oscap`{.literal} and `autotailor`{.literal} command-line tools or Red Hat Lightspeed for both tailoring and scanning. For more information, see [Managing SCAP security policies in the Red Hat Lightspeed compliance service](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_lightspeed/1-latest/html/assessing_and_monitoring_security_policy_compliance_of_rhel_systems/compliance-managing-policies).

SCAP Security Guide

:   The `scap-security-guide`{.literal} package does not contain the following profiles:

    -   Protection Profile for General Purpose Operating Systems (OSPP)
    -   Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) - Basic
    -   Centro Criptológico Nacional (CCN) - Intermediate

    For the complete list of profiles supported in RHEL 10, see [SCAP security profiles supported in RHEL 10](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/security_hardening/scanning-the-system-for-configuration-compliance#scap-security-guide-profiles-supported-in-rhel-10).

### [20.2. Changes to cryptographic components](#changes-to-cryptographic-components) {#changes-to-cryptographic-components .title}

Review the most notable changes to cryptographic components between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

`ca-certificates`{.literal} truststore moved
:   The `/etc/pki/tls/certs`{.literal} truststore is converted to a different format better optimized for OpenSSL. As a consequence, if you use the files in `/etc/pki/tls/certs`{.literal} directly, switch to the `/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted`{.literal} directory, where the same data is stored. For example, software that accesses the trust bundle at `/etc/pki/tls/certs/ca-bundle.crt`{.literal} should switch to using `/etc/pki/ca-trust/extracted/pem/tls-ca-bundle.pem`{.literal} instead.

`fips-mode-setup`{.literal} is removed
:   The `fips-mode-setup`{.literal} command is removed from RHEL. To enable the cryptographic module self-checks mandated by the Federal Information Processing Standard (FIPS) 140, enable FIPS mode during the system installation. See the [Switching RHEL to FIPS mode chapter](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/security_hardening/switching-rhel-to-fips-mode) in the *Security hardening* document for more information.

`/etc/system-fips`{.literal} removed
:   Support for indicating FIPS mode through the `/etc/system-fips`{.literal} file has been removed from RHEL. To install RHEL in FIPS mode, add the `fips=1`{.literal} parameter to the kernel command line during the system installation. You can check whether RHEL operates in FIPS mode by displaying the `/proc/sys/crypto/fips_enabled`{.literal} file.

`compat-openssl11`{.literal} is removed
:   The compatibility library for OpenSSL 1.1, `compat-openssl11`{.literal}, has been removed from RHEL 10. OpenSSL 1.1 is no longer maintained upstream and applications that use the OpenSSL TLS toolkit should be migrated to version 3.x.

`pkcs11-provider`{.literal} replaces `openssl-pkcs11`{.literal}
:   As a part of the migration from OpenSSL engines to the Providers API, the `pkcs11-provider`{.literal} package replaces the `openssl-pkcs11`{.literal} package (`engine_pkcs11`{.literal}). The `openssl-pkcs11`{.literal} package is removed from RHEL 10.

`DEFAULT`{.literal} cryptographic policy rejects TLS ciphers with RSA key exchange

:   TLS ciphers that use the RSA key exchange are no longer accepted in the `DEFAULT`{.literal} system-wide cryptographic policy in RHEL 10. These ciphers do not provide perfect forward secrecy and are not considered as secure as ciphers that use other key exchanges, for example, the Elliptic-curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange.

    This change also reduces the exposure to side-channel attacks because the RSA key exchange uses PKCS #1 v1.5 encryption padding, which can cause vulnerability to timing side-channel attacks.

    If you need the RSA key exchange for interoperability with legacy systems, you can re-enable it by using the LEGACY system-wide cryptographic policy or by applying a custom subpolicy.

The `LEGACY`{.literal} cryptographic policy disallows SHA-1 signatures in TLS
:   The `LEGACY`{.literal} system-wide cryptographic policy in RHEL 10 no longer allows creating or verifying signatures that use SHA-1 in TLS contexts. Therefore, libraries other than OpenSSL might no longer accept or create any signatures that use SHA-1 regardless of use case. OpenSSL continues to accept signatures that use SHA-1 when not used for TLS if the system is in `LEGACY`{.literal} or this functionality is re-enabled with a custom subpolicy.

`SHA1`{.literal} subpolicy removed
:   The `SHA1`{.literal} subpolicy that allowed to use the SHA-1 algorithm for creating and verifying signatures in the `DEFAULT`{.literal} system-wide cryptographic policy after entering the `update-crypto-policies --set DEFAULT:SHA1`{.literal} command is no longer available in RHEL 10.

OpenSSL no longer permits SHA-1 at `SECLEVEL=2`{.literal} in TLS
:   OpenSSL does not accept the SHA-1 algorithm at `SECLEVEL=2`{.literal} in TLS in RHEL 10. If your scenario requires using TLS 1.0 or 1.1, you must explicitly set `SECLEVEL=0`{.literal} and switch to the LEGACY system-wide cryptographic policy. In the LEGACY policy, applications that use SHA-1 in signatures outside of TLS will continue to work.

OpenSSL cipher suites no longer enable cipher suites with disabled hashes or MACs
:   Previously, applying custom cryptographic policies could leave certain TLS 1.3 cipher suites enabled even if their hashes or MACs were disabled, because the OpenSSL TLS 1.3-specific `Ciphersuites`{.literal} option values were controlled only by the `ciphers`{.literal} option of the cryptographic policy. With this update, `crypto-policies`{.literal} takes more algorithms into account when deciding whether to enable a cipher suite. As a result, OpenSSL on systems with custom cryptographic policies might refuse to negotiate some of the previously enabled TLS 1.3 cipher suites in better accordance with the system configuration.

OpenSSL FIPS indicators are subject to change during the RHEL 10 lifetime
:   Because RHEL introduced OpenSSL FIPS indicators before the OpenSSL upstream did, and both designs differ, the indicators may change in a future minor version of RHEL 10. After the potential adoption of the upstream API, the RHEL 10.0 indicators might return an error message \"unsupported\" instead of a result. See the [OpenSSL FIPS Indicators](https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/master/doc/designs/fips_indicator.md) GitHub document for details.

OpenSSL 3.5 uses standard format for ML-KEM and ML-DSA

:   In RHEL 10.0, the `oqsprovider`{.literal} library used a pre-standard format for the Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) and the Module-Lattice-Based Digital Signature Algorithm (ML-DSA) private keys. With the rebase to OpenSSL 3.5, you must convert the ML-KEM and ML-DSA keys to the standard format by using the following command:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    # openssl pkcs8 -in <old_private_key> -nocrypt -topk8 -out <standard_private_key>
    ```

    Replace `<old_private_key>`{.literal} with the path to the non-standard private key, and `<standard_private_key>`{.literal} with the path where the standard key will be saved.

Switching to LEGACY policy does not enable support for SHA-1 in TLS connections

:   You can control support for SHA-1 signatures either by the `@SECLEVEL`{.literal} setting specified in the default cipher string or the `rh-allow-sha1-signatures`{.literal} property. Support for SHA-1 in the TLS context is enabled by setting `@SECLEVEL=0`{.literal}. However, this setting also allows other insecure algorithms.

    You can override the `SECLEVEL`{.literal} setting by specifying the `rh-allow-sha1-signatures`{.literal} property in the `evp_properties`{.literal} section. By default and when unspecified in the configuration file, `evp_properties`{.literal} is set to `no`{.literal}. The system-wide cryptographic policies set the property to `yes`{.literal} after you switch to the `LEGACY`{.literal} policy.

    Therefore, to enable support for SHA-1 in contexts outside TLS, you can switch the system to the `LEGACY`{.literal} cryptographic policy. To enable SHA-1 in TLS, you must switch the system to `LEGACY`{.literal} and use a cipher string that sets `@SECLEVEL=0`{.literal} either by defining a custom cryptographic policy or setting this for your application in OpenSSL.

Stricter SSH host key permissions have been restored
:   The necessary host key permissions have been changed from the previous less strict value of `0640`{.literal} to `0600`{.literal}, which is also the value used upstream. The `ssh_keys`{.literal} group, which previously owned all SSH keys, has also been removed. Therefore, the `ssh-keysign`{.literal} utility uses the SUID bit instead of the SGID bit.

`crypto-policies`{.literal} now set `allow-rsa-pkcs1-encrypt = false`{.literal} for GnuTLS
:   In RHEL 10, the GnuTLS library blocks encryption and decryption with the RSA PKCS #1 v1.5 padding by default. Except for the LEGACY policy, the `allow-rsa-pkcs1-encrypt = false`{.literal} option is specified in all system-wide cryptographic policies (DEFAULT, FUTURE, and FIPS).

Non-post-quantum KEX removed from the `FUTURE`{.literal} policy

:   The `FUTURE`{.literal} system-wide cryptographic policy no longer allows traditional, non-post-quantum, key exchange (KEX) methods. With this update, you can use only hybrid Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) key exchange algorithms.

    This aligns with the target use of the `FUTURE`{.literal} policy in controlled, isolated deployments and significantly impacts interoperability with the public internet. For example, when you switch RHEL 10 to the `FUTURE`{.literal} policy, you cannot connect to the cdn.redhat.com network. Also, Java clients cannot connect to TLS servers running in `FUTURE`{.literal}.

    Note that upcoming RHEL releases might further restrict signature algorithms in certificates and signatures to allow only post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in the `FUTURE`{.literal} policy.

`libssh`{.literal} supports hybrid key exchange with ML-KEM and `crypto-policies`{.literal} enable `mlkem768x25519-sha256`{.literal} by default

:   Starting from RHEL 10.2, the `libssh`{.literal} library introduces support for post-quantum traditional (PQ/T) hybrid key exchange methods based on the quantum-resistant Module-Lattice-Based Key-Encapsulation Mechanism (ML-KEM) standard and traditional Elliptic-curve Diffie--Hellman (ECDH) key exchange schemes. The `mlkem768x25519-sha256`{.literal} algorithm is the preferred key exchange method for SSH connections unless you change the configuration.

    Also, the system-wide cryptographic policies enable the `mlkem768x25519-sha256`{.literal} key exchange algorithms for the `libssh`{.literal} library in all predefined policies. As a result, `mlkem768x25519-sha256`{.literal} is enabled by default and negotiated with the highest priority, protecting SSH connections with a combination of traditional and post-quantum cryptography (PQC).

### [20.3. Changes to SELinux](#changes-to-selinux) {#changes-to-selinux .title}

Review the most notable changes to SELinux between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

SELinux file context equivalency for `/var/opt`{.literal} overrides custom rules during system upgrades

:   Starting with RHEL 10.2, the SELinux policy treats the `/var/opt`{.literal} path as equivalent to the `/opt`{.literal} path. Because equivalency rules take priority over explicit paths, with this update, files under `/var/opt`{.literal} inherit default `/opt`{.literal} security contexts, such as `usr_t`{.literal}.

    This change impacts systems upgraded from earlier RHEL releases. Custom or third-party file context rules defined directly for `/var/opt`{.literal} are ignored after upgrading to RHEL 10.2. As a result, applications or utilities, such as `logrotate`{.literal} or monitoring agents, that rely on custom contexts under `/var/opt`{.literal}, might encounter SELinux denials or service failures.

    To set custom SELinux contexts for specific subdirectories under `/var/opt`{.literal}, define local `fcontext`{.literal} rules for the corresponding `/opt`{.literal} directory structure, then apply the changes on the corresponding `/var/opt`{.literal} directory structure by using the `restorecon`{.literal} command:

    ``` {.language-shell-session tabindex="-1"}
    # semanage fcontext -a -t <context_type> "/opt/<directory>(/.*)?"
    # restorecon -R -v /var/opt/<directory>
    ```

SELinux policy modules related to EPEL packages moved to `-extra`{.literal} subpackages in the CRB repository

:   In RHEL 10.0, the SELinux policy modules related only to packages contained in the Extra Packages for Enterprise Linux (EPEL) repository and not to any RHEL package were moved from the `selinux-policy`{.literal} package to the `selinux-policy-epel`{.literal} package. This reduced the size of `selinux-policy`{.literal}, allowing the system to perform operations such as rebuilding and loading the SELinux policy faster.

    In RHEL 10.1, the modules from `selinux-policy-epel`{.literal} are moved to the following `-extra`{.literal} subpackages in the RHEL CodeReady Linux Builder (CRB) repository:

    -   `selinux-policy-targeted-extra`{.literal}
    -   `selinux-policy-mls-extra`{.literal}

    This change enables the automatic installation of `-extra`{.literal} SELinux policy modules when users enable the EPEL repository.

`rpm -ql`{.literal} returns incorrect location of the `selinux-policy`{.literal} packages on RHEL in image mode
:   The `rpm -ql`{.literal} command lists non-existent locations of the `selinux-policy`{.literal} and `selinux-policy-targeted`{.literal} when used on RHEL in image mode. The policy modules are installed in the `/etc/selinux/targeted`{.literal} instead of `/var/lib/selinux/targeted`{.literal} directory, as misleadingly reported by `rpm`{.literal}. This discrepancy is expected because most file systems in image mode are read-only, and the RPM tool doesn't have the actual location of installed packages.

## [Chapter 21. Shells and command-line tools](#shells-and-command-line-tools) {#chapter-21.-shells-and-command-line-tools .title}

Review the most notable changes to shells and command-line tools between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

### [21.1. Notable changes to system management](#changes-to-system-management) {#notable-changes-to-system-management .title}

Review the most notable changes to system management between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

The `perl(Mail::Sender)`{.literal} module has been removed
:   The `perl(Mail::Sender)`{.literal} module is removed from RHEL 10 without any replacement. As a consequence, the `checkbandwidth`{.literal} script from `net-snmp-perl`{.literal} package does not support email alerts when bandwidth high/low levels for a host or interface are reached.

### [21.2. Notable changes to command line tools](#notable-changes-to-command-line-tools) {#notable-changes-to-command-line-tools .title}

Review the most notable changes to command line tools between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

`cgroupsv1`{.literal} is a removed functionality in RHEL 10
:   `cgroups`{.literal} is a kernel subsystem used for process tracking, system resource allocation, and partitioning. In previous versions, `systemd`{.literal} service manager supported booting in the `cgroups v1`{.literal} and in `cgroups v2`{.literal} mode (with v1 as the default in rhel8 and v2 as the default in rhel9). In Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10, `systemd`{.literal} will no longer support booting in the `cgroups v1`{.literal} mode; only `cgroups v2`{.literal} mode will be available.

RHEL 10 provides ReaR in version 2.9

:   The ReaR utility has been upgraded to version 2.9. The notable changes include:

    -   On IBM Z, the `IPL`{.literal} output method is now deprecated. The `RAMDISK`{.literal} output method is provided as an alternative. The `OUTPUT=RAMDISK`{.literal} functionality is identical on all the supported hardware architectures, unlike the deprecated `OUTPUT=IPL`{.literal} functionality, which is specific to IBM System Z.

        Note that the names of the recovery ramdisk image and the kernel that are generated by ReaR are different with `OUTPUT=RAMDISK`{.literal}. The kernel is named `kernel-$RAMDISK_SUFFIX`{.literal} and the ramdisk image is named `initramfs-$RAMDISK_SUFFIX.img`{.literal}. The `RAMDISK_SUFFIX`{.literal} is a configuration variable that you can set in `/etc/rear/local.conf`{.literal}. If the variable is not set, it defaults to the host name of the system. If you used the `OUTPUT=IPL`{.literal} setting with previous ReaR versions, change it to `OUTPUT=RAMDISK`{.literal} and adjust any automation that uses the resulting kernel and ramdisk image files according to the new naming convention described above to be compatible with future ReaR versions when the `IPL`{.literal} output method is removed.

    -   The default value of the `ISO_VOLID`{.literal} configuration variable, which specifies the label of the resulting ISO image when using the `OUTPUT=ISO`{.literal} setting, was changed to `REAR-ISO`{.literal}. The default in previous ReaR versions was `RELAXRECOVER`{.literal}. If you need to mount the resulting ISO 9660 file system by label, adjust the `mount`{.literal} command for the label change. Alternatively, you can set the `ISO_VOLID`{.literal} variable in `/etc/rear/local.conf`{.literal} to `RELAXRECOVER`{.literal} to restore the former behavior.

`mkfs.xfs`{.literal} requires a minimum XFS file system size of 300 MB
:   The `mkfs.xfs`{.literal} tool from the `xfsprogs`{.literal} package shipped in RHEL 10 requires XFS file systems to have a minimum size of 300 MB to avoid performance and redundancy issues. For more information, see the [Upstream documentation](https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/fs/xfs/xfsprogs-dev.git/commit/?id=6e0ed3d19c54603f0f7d628ea04b550151d8a262). If you must create a file system smaller than 300 MB, use the `ext4`{.literal} file system instead.

## [Chapter 22. Software management](#software-management) {#chapter-22.-software-management .title}

Review the most notable changes to software management between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

### [22.1. Notable changes to DNF](#notable-changes-to-dnf) {#notable-changes-to-dnf .title}

Review the most notable changes to DNF between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Modularity is deprecated

:   In RHEL 10, the modularity functionality is deprecated and will be removed in a future major release. Therefore, the DNF `module`{.literal} command displays a deprecation warning.

    Note

    In previous RHEL major versions, some Application Streams were available as modules as an extension to the RPM format. In RHEL 10, Red Hat does not intend to provide any Application Streams that use modularity as the packaging technology. Therefore, no modular content is being distributed with RHEL 10.

The repository metadata is not downloaded by default

:   Previously, when you downloaded a repository's metadata, the filelists metadata was downloaded by default. The filelists metadata is large and is typically not needed. With this update, this metadata is not downloaded by default, which improves responsiveness and saves disk space. The filelists metadata is also no longer downloaded or updated from repositories and is not loaded into the DNF transaction when you run a `dnf`{.literal} command. If the `dnf`{.literal} command requires the filelists metadata or includes a file-related argument, the metadata is loaded automatically.

    Note

    When a package has a filepath dependency that requires filelists metadata to be resolved, the transaction fails with a dependency resolution error and the following hint:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    (try to add '--skip-broken' to skip uninstallable packages or '--setopt=optional_metadata_types=filelists' to load additional filelists metadata)
    ```

    Note

    If you want to re-enable the default filelist metadata downloading, you can add the `filelists`{.literal} value to the `optional_metadata_types`{.literal} option in the `/etc/dnf/dnf.conf`{.literal} configuration file.

The DNF `debug`{.literal} plugin is removed

:   The DNF `debug`{.literal} plugin, which included the `dnf debug-dump`{.literal} and `dnf debug-restore`{.literal} commands, is removed from the `dnf-plugins-core`{.literal} package. Depending on your scenario, you can use the following commands instead:

    -   `dnf list --installed`{.literal} or `dnf repoquery --installed`{.literal} to list packages installed on your system

    -   `dnf repolist -v`{.literal} to list repositories enabled on your system

    -   `dnf install $(</tmp/list)`{.literal} to replicate packages installed on a source system to the target system. For example:

        1.  Save a list of packages installed on a source system into the `/tmp/list`{.literal} file:

            ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
            $ dnf repoquery --installed >/tmp/list
            ```

        2.  Copy the `/tmp/list`{.literal} file to the target system.

        3.  Replicate packages on the target system:

            ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
            $ dnf install $(</tmp/list)"
            ```

The support for the `libreport`{.literal} library is removed
:   The support for the `libreport`{.literal} library is removed from DNF. If you want to attach DNF logs to your bug reports, you need to do it manually or by using a different mechanism.

`dnf-plugins-core`{.literal} rebased to version 4.7.0
:   The `dnf-plugins-core`{.literal} package is rebased to version 4.7.0 that provides a new `python3-dnf-plugin-pre-transaction-actions`{.literal} package. This package includes a new `pre-transaction-actions`{.literal} DNF plugin that allows you to run a command upon starting an RPM transaction. For more information, see the `dnf-pre-transaction-actions(8)`{.literal} manual page on your system.

### [22.2. Notable changes to createrepo_c](#notable-changes-to-createrepo-c) {#notable-changes-to-createrepo_c .title}

Review the most notable changes to `createrepo_c`{.literal} between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Default `createrepo_c`{.literal} compression changed from `gzip`{.literal} to `Zstandard`{.literal}
:   The `createrepo_c`{.literal} command compresses non-database metadata with the `Zstandard`{.literal} (`zstd`{.literal}) compression algorithm instead of `gzip`{.literal}. Note that the database metadata still defaults to the `bzip2`{.literal} format. You can override the compression format by using the `--general-compress-type`{.literal} option.

SQLite databases are not generated by default

:   To save disk space, the `createrepo_c`{.literal} command no longer creates SQLite databases next to XML files. You can explicitly create the databases by using the `--database`{.literal} option.

    Note

    Support for creating the SQLite databases with the `createrepo --databases`{.literal} command is deprecated and will be removed in future RHEL major versions.

### [22.3. Notable changes to RPM](#notable-changes-to-rpm) {#notable-changes-to-rpm .title}

Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 is distributed with RPM version 4.19. This version introduces many enhancements over its previous versions.

#### [22.3.1. Improved user experience and security](#rpm-user-experience-and-security) {#improved-user-experience-and-security .title}

Review the improvements to user experience and security between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

A new OpenPGP back end based on Sequoia
:   RPM uses Sequoia PGP for the verification of package signatures, which replaces the legacy OpenPGP parser. Sequoia PGP is a modern, Rust-based implementation of the OpenPGP standard that focuses on safety and robustness.

Major updates to cryptography

:   RHEL 10.1 introduces the following updates to RPM cryptography, which provide major security enhancements to signing and verifying RPM packages:

    -   Support for multiple signatures in a package
    -   Support for the new OpenPGP (RFC-9580) standard
    -   Support for post-quantum cryptography (PQC) in RPM packages. PQC is a set of algorithms that should withstand the attacks of quantum computers, enhancing software security. To sign a package with PQC algorithms, you can use Sequoia PGP software.

    For more information, see [Signing RPM packages with Sequoia PGP by using PQC](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/packaging_and_distributing_software/packaging-software-with-rpm#signing-packages-with-pqc).

`rpmsign --addsign`{.literal} no longer replaces existing signatures in an RPM package
:   Before this update the `rpmsign --addsign`{.literal} command replaced any existing signatures in an RPM package. Starting from RHEL 10.1, `rpmsign --addsign`{.literal} only adds new signatures and never deletes any. If an identical signature is already present in a package, RPM prints an error message and keeps the existing signature untouched.

A new `rpmlua`{.literal} command-line tool
:   This tool runs the RPM Lua interpreter in a standalone way that you can use for the development and testing of Lua scriptlets and macros. For more information, see the `rpmlua(8)`{.literal} man page on your system.

A new `rpmsort`{.literal} command-line tool
:   This tool allows you to sort RPM versions passed on standard input, similar to `sort(1)`{.literal} but with the awareness of RPM versioning scheme. For more information, see the `rpmsort(8)`{.literal} man page on your system.

A new `dbus-announce`{.literal} plugin
:   This plugin writes basic information about RPM transactions to the system D-Bus, for example, when packages are installed or removed. Other programs can subscribe to these signals to be notified of such events.

Downgrade support in `--freshen`{.literal} mode
:   Previously, you could use the `--freshen`{.literal} option only to upgrade packages that were already installed and skip packages that were not installed. With this enhancement, you can also use this operation to downgrade such packages. To do this, combine the `--freshen`{.literal} (`F`{.literal}) option with the `--oldpackage`{.literal} option.

#### [22.3.2. Improved packaging experience](#rpm-packaging-experience) {#improved-packaging-experience .title}

Review the improvements to the packaging experience between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

Support for dynamic `spec`{.literal} generation
:   You can add subpackages during the build process by placing files containing `spec`{.literal} parts into a predefined location. For more information, see [Dynamic Spec Generation](https://rpm-software-management.github.io/rpm/manual/dynamic_specs.html).

A new `--shell`{.literal} option in the `rpmspec`{.literal} command-line tool
:   This option runs an interactive RPM macro interpreter that you can use for the development and testing of RPM macros, either in or outside of the context of a `spec`{.literal} file. For more information, see the `rpmspec(8)`{.literal} man page on your system.

Support for applying individual patches in `%autopatch`{.literal}
:   You can list specific patch numbers as positional arguments, for example, `%autopatch 1 4 6`{.literal} to apply patch numbers 1, 4 and 6.

Proper shell-like globbing and escaping in the `%files`{.literal} section
:   Wildcard patterns and escaping characters, such as backslashes and quotes, in filenames are interpreted in a more conventional way, mirroring the behavior of shell interpreters such as Bash. Previously, undocumented limitations and exceptions to these rules could have unexpected results and could prevent the use of more complex patterns in the `%files`{.literal} section of a `spec`{.literal} file.

A new tag in source RPM packages containing the parsed and expanded contents of the `spec`{.literal} file
:   To help with analyzing packaging issues, a new `RPMTAG_SPEC`{.literal} tag is added to source RPM packages. This tag includes the contents of the expanded `spec`{.literal} file in the form used during the build. You can view this tag by running the `rpm --qf ‘%{spec}’ -q /path/to/my/src.rpm`{.literal} command.

Build parallelism considers system resources

:   RPM considers the available physical memory and address space when estimating the number of parallel processes and threads to use when building packages. This helps to prevent performance issues or build failures on systems with constrained resources, such as systems with a large number of CPUs but a limited amount of memory.

    You can adjust these estimates by specifying the amount of memory a single process or thread is assumed to require for your build by defining the `%_smp_tasksize_proc`{.literal} and `%_smp_tasksize_thread`{.literal} macros, respectively. Both macros have the default value of 512 MB. For example, if your system has performance issues, you can increase these values for RPM to allocate fewer CPUs for the build. Likewise, if your system is underutilized, you can decrease these values for RPM to allocate more CPUs.

    For more information, see [Macros for controlling build parallelism](https://rpm-software-management.github.io/rpm/manual/buildprocess.html#parallelism).

Payload compression with `zstd`{.literal} supports multi-threading
:   The `zstdio`{.literal} compression method accepts an optional `T`{.literal} parameter that specifies the number of threads to use when compressing payload during the build. This can help reduce the build time of large packages. To enable this feature, set the `%_binary_payload`{.literal} and `%_source_payload`{.literal} macros accordingly. For more information, see the associated comment block in the `/usr/lib/rpm/macros`{.literal} file and the [expected format table](https://ftp.osuosl.org/pub/rpm/api/4.19.0/group__rpmio.html#example-mode-strings).

A new optional `%conf`{.literal} `spec`{.literal} file section
:   You can use this section to configure the unpacked sources for building instead of configuring them in the `%prep`{.literal} or `%build`{.literal} sections of a `spec`{.literal} file.

Lua-native macro integration

:   The embedded Lua interpreter is updated to include the following enhancements:

    -   Easy access to options and arguments through Lua tables

        Previously, you had to use the `rpm.expand()`{.literal} function to access the options and arguments of parametric Lua macros. With this enhancement, these macros receive their options and arguments as the `opt`{.literal} and `arg`{.literal} local tables, respectively.

    -   Simplified access to macros

        Macros can be accessed through the `macros`{.literal} table in the global Lua environment. This table can also be used to call parametric macros, including all built-in macros.

    -   New bindings for RPM version objects and I/O streams

        You can create objects from RPM version strings by using the new `rpm.ver()`{.literal} function. You can use these objects to perform the following actions:

        -   Obtain the individual pre-parsed EVR components through the `e`{.literal}, `v`{.literal}, and `r`{.literal} fields, respectively.
        -   Compare RPM version strings to each other.

        You can also use the new `rpm.open()`{.literal} function to open file streams that use RPM's I/O features, such as transparent compression and decompression.

    For more information, see [Lua in RPM](https://rpm-software-management.github.io/rpm/manual/lua.html).

New macros for convenient string operations implemented in Lua
:   You can perform basic string operations, such as extracting a substring or obtaining the length, directly by using RPM macros, without having to run shell subprocesses. For more information, see [String operations](https://rpm-software-management.github.io/rpm/manual/macros.html#string-operations).

Unified calling conventions for built-in and user-defined macros
:   The `%foo arg`{.literal}, `%{foo arg}`{.literal}, and `%{foo:arg}`{.literal} notations used for calling macros are equivalent. Note, however, that there might still be minor exceptions and differences.

Multiple new built-in macros

:   Multiple new built-in macros are available, most notably:

    -   `%{rpmversion}`{.literal} for obtaining the version of RPM installed on the system.
    -   `%{exists:…​}`{.literal} for testing a file's existence.
