    -   `%{shescape:…​}`{.literal} for encompassing a string in single quotes (`''`{.literal}) for use in a shell command that expects a single argument.

New `%preuntrans`{.literal} and `%postuntrans`{.literal} scriptlets

:   The `%preuntrans`{.literal} and `%postuntrans`{.literal} uninstall-time scriptlets complement the existing install-time `%pretrans`{.literal} and `%posttrans`{.literal} scriptlets:

    -   `%preuntrans`{.literal} scriptlets are executed before a transaction for packages that this transaction will remove.
    -   `%postuntrans`{.literal} scriptlets are executed after a transaction for packages that this transaction removed.

Support for signing packages with Sequoia PGP is available as a Technology Preview

:   The `macros.rpmsign-sequoia`{.literal} macro file that configures RPM to use Sequoia PGP instead of GnuPG for signing packages is available as a Technology Preview. To enable its usage, perform the following steps:

    1.  Install the following packages:

        ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
        # dnf install rpm-sign sequoia-sq
        ```

    2.  Copy the `macros.rpmsign-sequoia`{.literal} file to the `/etc/rpm/`{.literal} directory:

        ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
        $ cp /usr/share/doc/rpm/macros.rpmsign-sequoia /etc/rpm/
        ```

#### [22.3.3. Other notable changes](#rpm-notable-changes) {#other-notable-changes .title}

Review the following notable changes to RPM between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

User and group name resolution is strictly local in alternate root operations
:   When installing or verifying packages in an alternate root directory specified with the `--root`{.literal} option, RPM obtains the UID (User Identifier) and GID (Group Identifier) numbers from the `passwd(5)`{.literal} and `group(5)`{.literal} files inside the target root directory, respectively, as opposed to using the Name Service Switch (NSS).

File ownership information is never obtained from the build system context
:   When building packages, the `%defattr`{.literal} directive interprets the dash (`-`{.literal}) placeholder for the user and group attributes as `root`{.literal}, instead of obtaining the actual ownership information from disk. Similarly, files in source RPM packages, such as `spec`{.literal} files, source archives, or patch files, are always owned by the root user and group, regardless of their ownership on disk.

The build tree (`%_builddir`{.literal}) is removed by default after a successful build
:   Previously, `rpmbuild(8)`{.literal} only cleaned up the build directory in the `--rebuild`{.literal} mode, not in the more commonly used modes, such as `-bb`{.literal}. Consequently, multiple packages being built caused the unnecessary accumulation of files over time. With this enhancement, if you prefer to always keep the build tree, for example, to investigate a non-fatal build issue, you can use the `--noclean`{.literal} option.

The `%patch`{.literal} directive must explicitly specify the patch numbers to apply

:   You can specify the patch number either of the following ways:

    -   By using the `-P`{.literal} option, for example, `%patch -P1 -P2`{.literal} to apply patch numbers 1 and 2.
    -   By passing the patch numbers as positional arguments, for example, `%patch 1 2`{.literal} to apply patch numbers 1 and 2.

    Important

    The `%patchN`{.literal} syntax, where `N`{.literal} is the patch number to apply, is deprecated.

    Note

    If no explicit patch number is specified with the `%patch`{.literal} directive, the build terminates with an error.

    Note

    It is recommended that you use the `%autosetup`{.literal} macro whenever possible, instead of applying the individual patches manually with the `%patch`{.literal} directive. When you use `%autosetup`{.literal}, patches are applied automatically in the order identified by their patch numbers. As a result, the `spec`{.literal} file is easier to read and maintain. For more information, see [Automating patch application](https://rpm-software-management.github.io/rpm/manual/autosetup.html).

## [Chapter 23. System roles](#system-roles) {#chapter-23.-system-roles .title}

Review the most notable changes to system roles between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

RHEL 10 control nodes can only manage RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 nodes
:   RHEL 10 contains `ansible-core`{.literal} 2.16. This Ansible version supports managing RHEL 9 and RHEL 10 nodes.

RHEL 10 control nodes can temporarily configure SQL Server only on RHEL 7, 8 and 9 managed nodes
:   The `microsoft.sql.server`{.literal} system role contained in the `ansible-collection-microsoft-sql`{.literal} package will not support configuring SQL Server on RHEL 10 managed nodes until Microsoft provides support. For that time period, you can use the `microsoft.sql.server`{.literal} on RHEL 10 control nodes to configure SQL Server on RHEL 7, 8, and 9 managed nodes.

In-place upgrade phases automation with the `analysis`{.literal}, `remediate`{.literal}, and `upgrade`{.literal} Ansible roles

:   With this release, you can use the `analysis`{.literal}, `remediate`{.literal}, and `upgrade`{.literal} Ansible roles to automate the pre-upgrade and upgrade phases of the in-place upgrade. By using these Ansible roles, you can quickly and efficiently upgrade large numbers of systems, saving you time.

    For more information, see [Upgrading large deployments by using Ansible roles](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html/upgrading_from_rhel_9_to_rhel_10/upgrading-large-deployments-by-using-ansible-roles).

## [Chapter 24. Virtualization](#virtualization) {#chapter-24.-virtualization .title}

Review the most notable changes to virtualization between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

The `i440fx-rhel7.6`{.literal} machine type has been removed

:   In RHEL 10, the `i440fx-rhel7.6`{.literal} machine type for virtual machines (VMs) has been replaced by `i440fx-rhel10.0`{.literal}. As a consequence, VMs that use `i440fx-rhel7.6`{.literal} cannot boot after upgrading your host to RHEL 10. Similarly, live-migrating a VM that uses `i440fx-rhel7.6`{.literal} to a RHEL 10 host causes the VM to stop working.

    To verify the machine type of a VM, use the following command:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    # virsh dumpxml <vm-name> | grep "machine="

    <type arch='x86_64' machine='pc-i440fx-rhel7.6'>hvm</type>
    ```

    To ensure that a VM with the `i440fx-rhel7.6`{.literal} machine type can run on your RHEL 10 host, do the following:

    1.  Open the XML configuration of the VM:

        ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
        # virsh edit <vm_name>
        ```

    2.  On the `<type>`{.literal} line, change the `machine`{.literal} parameter to `pc-i440fx-rhel10.0`{.literal}.

    3.  Save and exit the VM configuration.

    Note that the `i440fx`{.literal} machine type has also become deprecated in RHEL 10, and will be removed completely in a future major version of RHEL.

`virt-v2v`{.literal} removes support for certain Red Hat products

:   In RHEL 10, the `virt-v2v`{.literal} tool can no longer convert virtual machines from a RHEL 5 Xen host to KVM.

    In addition, `virt-v2v`{.literal} no longer supports exporting virtual machines to Red Hat Virtualization (RHV). As a consequence, the following options are no longer available in `virt-v2v`{.literal}:

    -   `-o rhv-upload`{.literal}
    -   `-o rhv`{.literal}
    -   `-o vdsm`{.literal}

`virt-p2v`{.literal} conversion is not available
:   The `virt-p2v`{.literal} tool cannot be used to convert a physical machine into a KVM virtual machine for a RHEL 10 host. For instructions on using `virt-p2v`{.literal} for RHEL 7, RHEL 8, and RHEL 9, see [the Red Hat KnowledgeBase](https://access.redhat.com/node/2702281).

RDMA-based migration has become unsupported
:   In RHEL 10, migrating virtual machines (VMs) by using Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA) is no longer supported. Therefore, Red Hat highly discourages using the `rdma`{.literal} URI for VM migration.

Legacy CPU models are now removed

:   A significant number of CPU models that were deprecated in RHEL 9 have become unsupported, and can no longer be used in virtual machines (VMs) in RHEL 10. The removed models are as follows:

    -   For Intel: models before Intel Xeon 55xx and 75xx Processor families (also known as Nehalem)
    -   For AMD: models before AMD Opteron G4
    -   For IBM Z: models before IBM z14

    Note that several other CPU models, including Nehalem and Opteron G4, have become deprecated in RHEL 10, and will become unsupported in a future major release of RHEL. For a complete list of the deprecated CPU models, use the following command:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    /usr/libexec/qemu-kvm -cpu help | grep depre | grep -v - -v
    ```

    To check whether your VM is using a deprecated CPU model, use the `virsh dominfo`{.literal} utility, and look for a line similar to the following in the `Messages`{.literal} section:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    tainted: use of deprecated configuration settings
    deprecated configuration: CPU model 'Nehalem'
    ```

## [Chapter 25. The web console](#the-web-console) {#chapter-25.-the-web-console .title}

Review the most notable changes to the web console between RHEL 9 and RHEL 10.

The host switcher in the RHEL web console is deprecated

:   The host switcher that provides connections to multiple machines through SSH from a single RHEL web console session is deprecated and disabled by default. Due to the web technology limitations, this feature cannot be secure.

    In the short term, you can enable the host switcher after assessing the risks in your scenario with the `AllowMultiHost`{.literal} option in the `cockpit.conf`{.literal} file:

    ``` {.language-plaintext tabindex="-1"}
    [WebService]
    AllowMultiHost=yes
    ```

    As more secure alternatives, you can use:

    -   the web console login page (with the secure limit of one host in a web browser session)
    -   the Cockpit Client flatpak

Support for `pam_cockpit_cert`{.literal} removed
:   Starting with RHEL 10.2, which includes the `cockpit`{.literal} packages version 356, support for the `pam_cockpit_cert`{.literal} PAM module in the `/etc/pam.d/cockpit`{.literal} file, which has been redundant since version 248, is removed. If you still use the module in your configuration, you must remove it manually.

### [A.5. Packages with removed support](#packages-with-removed-support) {#a.5.-packages-with-removed-support .title}

Review packages that are distributed in a supported repository in RHEL 9 and in the CodeReady Linux Builder repository RHEL 10.

Certain packages in RHEL 10 are distributed through the CodeReady Linux Builder repository, which contains unsupported packages for use by developers.

Note

The following table contains packages that are supported in RHEL 9 but are not supported in RHEL 10.
